source_reference_files.observed: Low-key background and olive tabletop; food itself bright orange/glazed, which already sets a high-reflection commercial style.
Warm daylight high-key restaurant food plate with cream sauce and plated meat. It is not an actual tomato-and-egg cooking content reference.

confirmed_from_pixels: R1 both fish images contain specular highlights on skin and pools of sauce. Shiny surfaces are plausible for steamed fish. User preferred brighter/stronger subject Y despite more visible shine.
R2 both tomato-egg photos use distinct wet tomato surfaces and softer porous egg curds; user voted a tie. Generic 'make everything matte' would be incorrect.
R3 both bean dishes show many long bright reflections across green-bean skins, especially continuous streaks on multiple pods; food material may feel lacquered at full crop.
R3 VPD X shows localized browning/wrinkle cues and overall lower food exposure than direct Y, but its user preference was a tie. The single extra prompt did not deliver preferred overall appearance.
R3 XHS visual style reference itself has glossy sauced shrimp; it is not suitable as ground-truth for actual dry-fried bean microgeometry.
reasonable_hypotheses_not_proven: Transfer of shiny commercial-food visual style from source reference could contribute to glossy output; no isolation proves this is the cause.
Broad or repeated highlights may feel plasticky when they fail to follow ingredient surface orientation, but digital photos alone cannot establish true physical BRDF or actual cooking process.

Additional prompt text may have changed overall exposure rather than only bean specular geometry; measuring raw bright pixel ratios across differently exposed compositions is not a fair realism score.

The more promising leverage point may be selecting source photos with suitable material/rendering behavior and providing ingredient-correct physical reference, rather than injecting more 'avoid shine' terms.
